When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger

I should have protected others and I failed

issues.explanation: The profile only includes Memory and Negative Appraisals, with the formulation showing a strong reciprocal link specifically between these two nodes. The memory items are dominated by trauma-recall qualities and guilt on recall, but 'Body as Enemy' and especially the globally externalized appraisal 'Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you' shift toward current somatic threat/general danger beliefs that are not reflected in the memory content and are hard to reconcile with the otherwise memory-centred formulation. Given no active Threat or Trigger links, these appraisal items do not align well with the specified cognitive pattern.

issues.item: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
issues.explanation: This appraisal is hard to reconcile with the provided cognitive formulation. The only active connections are between Negative Appraisals and Memory, suggesting appraisals should be closely tied to trauma recollection and meaning-making about the event. A generalized interpersonal-danger belief ('You can never know who will harm you') implies an active Threat focus, yet Threat is otherwise unrepresented and all Threat-related edges are inactive. The other appraisal items are self-blaming and memory-linked (weakness, inaction guilt), so this one pulls the profile toward a different formulation not supported elsewhere.

vignette:
Roberto is a 55-year-old Navy officer of Colombian descent who has spent the better part of three decades navigating the disciplined hierarchies of military life. He is currently in a long-term relationship and presents to the clinic with a PCL-5 score of 70, describing a level of suffering he has concealed from colleagues and his partner for longer than he can precisely recall. What finally brought him to seek help was not a single crisis but an accumulating exhaustion - the sense, as he put it in the intake session, that he no longer trusts his own mind.

The precipitating event occurred several years ago when Roberto, then serving in a liaison capacity, found himself embedded with a civilian population in an active conflict zone. His role was advisory rather than combatant, which would later become the source of his deepest torment. During a sustained period of shelling, he witnessed the deaths of several civilians - including children - in a narrow street he had been moving through moments before. He had received fragmentary intelligence suggesting the area might be targeted, and he had not acted on it with the urgency it warranted. He had made a judgment call. The shelling came. He survived. They did not.

In the months that followed, Roberto found the memory did not behave like other memories. At times it returned with a completeness that erased the present entirely - the smell of dust and burning, the particular quality of the light, the sounds arriving in the wrong order, all of it simultaneous and total, as though his nervous system had never left that street. At other times, he could narrate the sequence of events in a flat, dissociated register, as if recounting something that had happened to a man he had read about, the facts present but the self entirely absent. Both modes frightened him, though in different ways.

What has become the central and self-reinforcing architecture of Roberto's suffering is the relationship between these intrusive memories and the appraisals that accompany them. He has come to believe, with a conviction that feels to him like moral clarity rather than distortion, that he is a weak person - that a stronger man, a better officer, would have acted faster, more decisively, and that those civilians would be alive. He is certain he will never forgive himself for his inaction. The belief that he failed to protect others who depended, even indirectly, on the competence of those around them has settled into something close to identity. When the full sensory memory returns - and it returns often - it does not arrive as a neutral recording but as evidence. Each reliving confirms the appraisal: here is the proof of what you are. The guilt that floods him in those moments is not incidental to the memory but woven into its texture, so that remembering and self-condemnation have become functionally inseparable.

The reverse is equally true, and equally relentless. When Roberto sits in briefings aboard his current posting and is called upon to make rapid assessments - precisely the professional demand his rank requires - the appraisals surface first. The thought that he is the kind of man who fails to act arrives before the memory itself, and then the memory follows, crowding out the present. His colleagues notice, occasionally, a pause before he speaks that seems inconsistent with his experience and rank. He has begun to volunteer less in operational discussions, finding reasons to defer, to consult, to delay - not out of genuine uncertainty but out of a fear that his judgment is irreparably compromised. This withdrawal has begun to affect how he is perceived professionally, which in turn deepens his conviction that he is not the officer - or the man - he once believed himself to be.

The emotionless recall, when it comes, offers no relief; it simply registers as further evidence of something broken in him. Roberto does not come to therapy hoping to feel better, exactly. What he most hopes for, expressed haltingly in the first session, is to understand how a single afternoon has come to constitute the whole of who he is - and what frightens him most is that it simply has.
